### Summary

CSV exports reproduced record values and column titles beginning with a formula character verbatim, so a spreadsheet application opening the exported file evaluated them as formulas.

### Details

The CSV serialiser in `export.service.ts` wrote the header row and every cell value into the export exactly as stored, without prefixing the values whose leading character a spreadsheet treats as the start of a formula - equals, plus, minus, at, tab and carriage return. Any text an attacker could place into a record therefore reached the file intact, as did any column title they could set, and the receiving spreadsheet parsed it as a formula rather than as text. The record path is reachable by anyone who can write a cell value, including an anonymous submitter of a public form attached to the exported table.

### Impact

Content supplied by a low-privileged collaborator or by an entirely anonymous form submitter executed as a spreadsheet formula in the context of whoever opened the export - typically a base owner or administrator on their own workstation. Depending on the spreadsheet application's settings and the user's response to its warning prompts, such a formula can read other local data, exfiltrate cell contents through an outbound request, or invoke an external command. No authentication is required where a public form feeds the exported view.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@hunntr](https://github.com/hunntr).
